idiom_name: sealed hierarchy plus exhaustive when (smart casts, destructuring) - compiler PSI for real source
implementation_notes: For a tree you own, Kotlin states the pattern directly: a sealed interface with data-class variants, an exhaustive when with smart casts and destructuring declarations as the pattern, and a recursive function as the engine - the compiler then proves that no node kind was forgotten, which is exactly what a pattern bag cannot do. Capture binding is a bound variable in the branch and the action is the branch body, so the classic rule table disappears into the match. When the subject is actual Kotlin source, the compiler PSI is the tool: KtVisitor and its KtTreeVisitorVoid subclass own the walk through KtElement.accept and acceptChildren, and a rule is an overridden visitKtElement or visitCallExpression with a type check, which requires kotlin-compiler-embeddable or the IntelliJ platform. Keep the sealed form for in-project trees and reach for PSI only when real source must be matched or rewritten.
pitfalls: Exhaustiveness holds only for sealed hierarchies and only when the when has no else branch; a tree built from Java classes or an open interface falls through silently, exactly like an unhandled pattern.
Rebuilding nodes on every pass allocates a new tree; fold once, share unchanged subtrees and compare references before copying, or the rewrite costs more than the analysis.

PSI traversal has no exhaustiveness: overriding visitKtElement means every unhandled node kind is skipped without a warning, so PSI rules need their own coverage tests and usually a sealed wrapper of their own.
